claims.text: Short-range chemical order governs both structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Locally ordered atomic clusters reduce atomic mobility.
Locally ordered atomic clusters prevent phase separation.
An oxygen sublattice in high-entropy oxides can serve as a buffer layer that improves structural robustness.
A buffering oxygen sublattice absorbs strain and accommodates configurational fluctuations.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloy is a nearly random solid solution with minimal pre-existing short-range order.
High-temperature annealing activates atomic diffusion and permits spontaneous development of short-range chemical order.
Al0.1CrCoFeNi exhibits chemical clustering and high-temperature short-range ordering.
(Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O possesses an oxygen sublattice capable of a buffering role.
Short-range ordered clusters absorb mechanical strain.
Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility, allowing atoms to form locally favorable clusters.
Cluster formation lowers the free-energy barrier against further diffusion.
Cluster formation lowers the free-energy barrier against phase transformation.
Local ordering mitigates extensive phase separation and maintains a homogeneous phase.
High-temperature annealing will increase measurable short-range order relative to lower-temperature processing.
The increase in short-range order will improve resistance to phase separation or decomposition.
Lower-temperature processing retains full configurational disorder because it does not permit significant atomic rearrangement.
The proposed mechanism applies only where diffusion is activated below melting and where the composition supports effective clustering or a buffering sublattice.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mediator state that ordering reduces atomic mobility, whereas the mechanism says clustering lowers the free-energy barrier against further diffusion, which would ordinarily facilitate rather than suppress diffusion.
The mechanism says clusters lower the barrier against phase transformation, while the predicted outcome requires increased resistance to phase transformation, decomposition, or separation.
